guide.summary: The most heavily weighted unit (20–30%). It connects short-run stabilization policy to long-run outcomes: combined fiscal and monetary policy, the short-run and long-run Phillips curves, the quantity theory of money, deficits and national debt, crowding out, and the determinants of long-run economic growth and supply-side policy.

sections.heading: Policy in the short run and the long run
sections.body: Fiscal and monetary policy can both shift AD. A policy mix can have offsetting or reinforcing effects (e.g., expansionary fiscal with contractionary monetary keeps output steady but raises interest rates). In the long run, output returns to potential (LRAS), so demand-side policy changes only the price level. Persistent attempts to keep unemployment below the natural rate lead to accelerating inflation.

sections.heading: The Phillips curve
sections.body: The short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment: AD increases move the economy up and left along the SRPC (lower unemployment, higher inflation); AD decreases move it down and right. The long-run Phillips curve (LRPC) is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment: there is no long-run tradeoff. SRPC shifts with inflation expectations and supply shocks: higher expected inflation or a negative supply shock (higher oil prices) shifts SRPC right/up; lower expected inflation or a positive supply shock shifts it left/down. Changes in the natural rate shift both LRPC and SRPC. An AD-AS point maps to a Phillips curve point: recessionary gap → right of LRPC; inflationary gap → left of LRPC.

sections.heading: Money growth and inflation
sections.body: Quantity theory of money: MV = PY (money × velocity = price level × real output). If velocity is stable and output is at potential, money growth translates into inflation in the long run (money is neutral in the long run). Hyperinflation results from excessive money creation, often to finance deficits.

sections.heading: Deficits, debt, and crowding out
sections.body: A budget deficit occurs when government spending exceeds revenue in a year; the national debt is the accumulation of past deficits minus surpluses. Expansionary fiscal policy increases deficits. Financing deficits by borrowing increases demand for loanable funds, raising real interest rates and reducing private investment (crowding out); higher rates can also reduce interest-sensitive consumption. Less investment means less capital accumulation and slower long-run growth. Large debts raise interest payments and can limit future policy options.

sections.heading: Economic growth
sections.body: Long-run growth is an increase in potential output, shown by LRAS and the PPC shifting right/out. Sources: more and better physical capital, human capital (education, training), technology, and natural resources; productivity (output per worker) is the key driver of rising living standards. Policies that promote growth: investment in infrastructure, education, and research; protection of property rights; tax incentives for saving and investment (supply-side policies). Growth rates compound: rule of 70 for doubling time.

keyTakeaways: SRPC: inverse inflation-unemployment tradeoff; LRPC vertical at natural rate.
Inflation expectations and supply shocks shift SRPC.
MV = PY; in the long run, money growth → inflation.
Deficits → higher real interest rates → crowding out.
Growth depends on capital, human capital, technology, productivity.
commonMistakes: Shifting the LRPC for AD changes.
Saying expansionary policy lowers unemployment permanently.
Using nominal interest rates for crowding out on the loanable funds graph.
Claiming economic growth is a movement from inside to on the PPC.
examTips: Translate between AD-AS and Phillips curve: inflationary gap ↔ left of LRPC.
Crowding-out FRQs need the loanable funds graph and the investment consequence.
For long-run growth, connect investment to capital stock to LRAS.
Quantity theory questions: hold V and Y constant unless told otherwise.
guide.cramSheet:
**Phillips:** SRPC down-sloping · LRPC vertical at NRU · ↑AD → up-left along SRPC

**SRPC shifts:** ↑expected inflation or negative supply shock → right/up

**Mapping:** recessionary gap → right of LRPC · inflationary gap → left

**Money:** MV = PY · long run: ↑M → ↑P only

**Fiscal LR:** deficit → ↑D_LF → ↑r → ↓I (crowding out) → slower growth

**Growth:** physical capital · human capital · technology · productivity · LRAS → right

practice.topic: 5.1–5.2 Stabilization Policy and the Phillips Curve
practice.prompt: Assume the economy of Veloria is in short-run equilibrium with real output above full-employment output. The central bank operates in a limited-reserves framework.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a correctly labeled AD-AS graph showing Veloria's current equilibrium, labeling the price level PL₁ and output Y₁.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify an open-market operation the central bank could use to address this situation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a correctly labeled money market graph showing the effect of the action in part (b) on the nominal interest rate.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the change in the interest rate affects aggregate demand, and state the effect on real output and the price level.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a correctly labeled Phillips curve graph showing Veloria's initial position (point A) and the effect of the central bank's policy (point B).

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: If instead the central bank takes no action, explain what happens to the short-run Phillips curve in the long run, and why.

rubric.description: Axes labeled price level and real GDP; AD, SRAS, and vertical LRAS.
AD-SRAS equilibrium at Y₁ to the right of LRAS (Y_f), with PL₁ labeled.
Axes nominal interest rate and quantity of money; downward-sloping MD and vertical MS.
MS shifts left, nominal interest rate rises.
Higher interest rates reduce investment and interest-sensitive consumption, so AD decreases; real output and price level decrease.
Axes inflation rate and unemployment rate; downward-sloping SRPC and vertical LRPC at the natural rate; point A on SRPC left of LRPC.
Point B on the same SRPC, down and to the right of A (higher unemployment, lower inflation).
Because workers and firms expect higher inflation, nominal wages rise (SRAS shifts left), so inflation expectations rise and unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The graph has 'Price Level' on the vertical axis and 'Real GDP' on the horizontal axis. Downward-sloping AD intersects upward-sloping SRAS at PL₁ and Y₁. A vertical LRAS is at Y_f, to the left of Y₁, showing an inflationary gap.

(b) The central bank should sell government bonds on the open market.

(c) The money market graph has 'Nominal Interest Rate' on the vertical axis and 'Quantity of Money' on the horizontal axis. MD slopes downward and MS is vertical. Selling bonds shifts MS to the left (MS₁ to MS₂), raising the nominal interest rate from i₁ to i₂.

(d) A higher interest rate makes borrowing more expensive, so investment spending and interest-sensitive consumption fall, decreasing AD. Real output and the price level both decrease.

(e) The Phillips curve graph has 'Inflation Rate' on the vertical axis and 'Unemployment Rate' on the horizontal axis. A vertical LRPC sits at the natural rate of unemployment. Point A is on the downward-sloping SRPC to the left of the LRPC (low unemployment, high inflation). Point B is lower and to the right on the same SRPC, closer to the LRPC.

(f) The SRPC shifts to the right. With the economy above full employment, workers expect continued high inflation and demand higher nominal wages. Rising wages shift SRAS left, so expected inflation rises, moving the SRPC up until unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate.
